Learning Objectives
Review the historical background and early designs of cemented and noncemented total knee
arthroplasty.
Review the indications for noncemented and cemented total knee arthroplasty.
Understand the importance of cement techniques on long-term component survivorship.
Discuss considerations for surgical techniques for noncemented total knee arthroplasty.
Recognize improvements in clinical outcomes with modern noncemented total knee
arthroplasty designs.

Cemented Total Knee Arthroplasty
Background
The total condylar prosthesis design introduced in 1973 became the prototype for several
contemporary design features and had much higher survivorship than earlier designs
(Resources 1, 2, and 3).

Background
The evolution of total knee arthroplasty (TKA) implants is best understood by reviewing
early concepts and designs. Early prototypes of TKA components, developed in the
1940s and 1950s, included a metallic interposition femoral mold used by Campbell in
1940; an acrylic tibial plateau prosthesis described by MacIntosh and Hunter1 in 1958;,
and the McKeever prosthesis, another metallic design that improved the success rates of
preceding implants. The first cemented TKA implant was the Gunston polycentric
bicondylar prosthesis developed in the 1960s by Freeman et al.2 With an emphasis on
lessening friction between components, sharing prosthesis loads across larger areas of
bone, and minimizing constraint (and thereby the risk of loosening), this device greatly
influenced implant design and technique. The first total condylar prosthesis, which was
designed by Insall et al3 and introduced in 1973, ushered in a new era of TKA. This
prosthesis not only established a new standard in survivorship that exceeded rates for
earlier designs (ie, reported to be >75% at a follow-up ranging from 15 to 20 years) but
also included symmetric femoral condyles and a highly congruent tibial polyethylene
component that resisted translation and dislocation. These features represented a leap
in TKA implant design and became the prototype for several contemporary device
features (Resource 4).
Patellar Components
Patellar components evolved from dome-shaped and single-peg configurations to more
anatomic designs with three peripheral pegs (Resource 5).
Compared with resurfaced patellas, nonresurfaced patellas have a higher reoperation rate.

In long-term follow-up studies, the leading causes of revision TKA were aseptic loosening
followed by infection.

Patellar Components
Early TKA implant designs did not account for the patella or for an asymmetric trochlea.
In 1972, Charles Townley4 was the first to introduce a patellar button in his cemented
anatomic TKA design. Since then, patellar designs have evolved from more dome-shaped
configurations to more anatomic configurations, with improved biomechanics and wear
properties. Fixation designs also evolved from single central pegs to three peripheral
pegs, which confer added rotational stability and are less likely to weaken the patella and
predispose it to fracture.
Routine resurfacing of the patella in TKA is controversial. A systematic review of 10 meta-
analyses comparing resurfacing with nonresurfacing demonstrated comparable
outcomes;5 however, another systematic review reported a higher revision surgery rate
in the nonresurfacing group (6.9%) than in the resurfacing group (1%) and lower clinical
outcome scores in the nonresurfacing group compared with the resurfacing group.6
These results should be interpreted with caution because it is easier to revise a TKA
implant for pain if the patella is unresurfaced, and the results of revision for isolated
patella resurfacing have been suboptimal.7-9
Long-term Outcomes of Modern Cemented TKA
The 20-year survivorship of modern cemented TKA implants is higher than 90%, including in
younger patient populations.
In cemented primary TKA, late aseptic loosening is attributed primarily to polyethylene wear
and osteolysis.

Long-term Outcomes of Modern Cemented TKA
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:52 PM
AAOS | Primary Total Knee Arthroplasty for Osteoarthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002065
3/19

Since the advent of cemented condylar TKA, several studies have documented excellent
20-year survivorship rates (>90% free of revision surgery) in patients with modern
implants.10-13 Registry data, particularly from Finnish and Australian registry databases,
have demonstrated excellent survivorship of certain modern TKA designs.14 Excellent
long-term clinical outcome scores and survivorship rates also have been observed in the
younger patient population, especially with the use of nonmodular tibial components.15
In long-term follow-up studies of earlier prostheses, the leading cause of revision TKA
was aseptic component loosening, which accounted for approximately 30% to 40% of
revision procedures and occurred more frequently than infection or instability.16,17
Infection remains a leading cause of failure in contemporary TKA designs.18,19
Historically, polyethylene wear and osteolysis also were major contributors to aseptic
failure; however, with improved tibial tray locking mechanisms and polyethylene
fabrication methods, these currently are less of a concern.7,20
The etiology of late aseptic loosening in cemented primary TKA likely is multifactorial,
including polyethylene wear and osteolysis and fatigue failure of the cement-bone
interface. The inherent inability of fixation to remodel over time predisposes it to failure
and loosening with repetitive loading. Another concern with certain designs and cement
viscosity applications is cement debonding from implants.21 This highlights the
importance of cement technique, including meticulous bony preparation and cement
pressurization, in promoting adequate interdigitation for durable fixation.
Cement Technique
Meticulous cementation technique is crucial to achieving long-term fixation of cemented
primary TKA components (Resource 6; Video 1).
Multiple techniques have been used to ensure adequate cement pressurization and achieve
durable cement fixation.

Video 1 Clarke HD: Cementation, from Lee GC, mod: How to perform a primary total knee


Cement Technique
Meticulous cement technique is critical to ensure adequate penetration and
interdigitation of the polymethyl methacralate bone cement into the cancellous bony
interface and provide a durable mechanical interlock. The bony surface must be free
from fat, blood, debris, and soft tissue, which may prevent adequate interdigitation.
Pulsatile irrigation typically is used to clean the bony surfaces, followed by drying before
cement application. A tibial sawbone model study examining the axial pull-out strength
of three different tibial baseplates demonstrated considerably decreased pull-out force
in all three designs if bovine marrow contents were applied to the surface before
cementation.22
Several techniques can be used to optimize cement fixation into host bone. Vacuum
mixing, rather than hand mixing, reduces the porosity of bone cement by eliminating air

bubbles. Structurally, this increases the fatigue strength of polymethyl methacralate and
may increase the longevity of implant fixation. Pressurization of bone cement into the
femoral and tibial canals and onto the bony surfaces can be achieved with the use of a
cement gun or via finger packing. Either technique is effective in achieving the ideal 3 to
4 mm of cement penetration into bone; however, for longer stems, pressurization with
the use of a cement gun likely is more effective. The cement must be in a relatively
doughy state to allow for adequate pressurization. In addition, some surgeons
recommend separate cementation of the femoral and tibial components rather than
simultaneous cementation, given that stress or range of motion of the knee during this
process may promote lipid infiltration into the cement-bone interface and weaken the
ultimate fixation strength. Finally, emerging evidence from a retrospective study of
institutional registry data on primary TKA suggested that the use of high-viscosity bone
cement was associated with a higher rate of aseptic loosening (1.9%) compared with the
use of a lower viscosity cement (0.92%), possibly related to decreased flow and bone
penetration.23
Noncemented TKA
Background
Noncemented fixation has the theoretic advantage of potential lifelong biologic fixation of TKA
components (Resource 7; Video 2).

6/19

Video 2 Levine BR: Cemented vs cementless TKA, from Levine BR, mod: The modern total knee
arthroplasty: What to make of all of these options. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, Las Vegas, NV, March 12-16, 2019.

Background
Although cemented fixation is the preferred technique for primary TKA, with excellent
clinical and radiographic outcomes reported at long-term follow-up, theoretic and
practical concerns are associated with its use. For example, the inherent lack of
remodeling in the cement-bone interface predisposes implants to fatigue failure because
of repetitive mechanical stress and loading over time, resulting in aseptic loosening,
particularly in younger, more active patients.16,24,25
Given the life span of cemented fixation and the increasing number of younger, more
active patients undergoing primary and revision TKA, interest in noncemented implants
has grown. Noncemented fixation is designed to provide durable and biologically active
fixation to host bone, with the capacity for remodeling over time. The main theoretic
advantage of this modality, especially in younger patients, is lifelong biologic fixation
with decreased risk of long-term aseptic loosening. In the current economic
environment, other potential advantages include operating room efficiency and implant

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002065
7/19

cost. Regardless, because of the failure of earlier noncemented implants, appropriate
indications for their use in modern TKA are controversial.
Early Noncemented Designs
Several initial noncemented TKA components had inherent flaws, leading to early failure. Tibial
and patellar components failed more frequently than femoral components.
Failure of early noncemented femoral components was related to fatigue fracture of the
implant and patellar maltracking.
In early noncemented tibial components, failure was multifactorial, including design limitations
that compromised initial stability and suboptimal porous coating because of thinner
polyethylene liners with inferior wear characteristics.
Early noncemented patellar components had high failure rates secondary to maltracking,
component dissociation, and polyethylene wear.

Early Noncemented Designs
The earliest TKA designs, incorporating noncemented vitallium cobalt-chromium alloy,
were developed in the 1940s, followed by the first noncemented condylar TKA design in
the 1970s, including the Kodama-Yamamoto and Imperial College?London Hospital
designs. However, noncemented designs did not become popular until the 1980s, at
which time a number of models entered the market. Over time and with close follow-up,
several design-related failures were discovered. Although noncemented femoral
components universally achieved fixation comparable to that of cemented designs, the
tibial and patellar components were the weak points of cementless fixation.
With the intimate geometric fit of noncemented femoral components, adequate initial
stability and subsequent osseointegration were achieved. Early failures typically resulted
from fatigue fractures in the thinner regions of the double-porous beaded surfaces of
the implant.26 In addition, older noncemented femoral component designs failed to
optimize patellar tracking, which contributed to patellar component failure.

8/19

Failure rates were considerably higher with early noncemented tibial components
because of inadequate osseointegration, aseptic loosening, and osteolysis, all of which
were related to early design issues. For example, the use of short pegs did not allow for
initial stability or prevent tray liftoff with weight bearing.27 Other designs used screws to
achieve initial stability, but this frequently resulted in screw tract osteolysis from
particulate debris infiltrating the metaphysis through an increased effective joint
space.28,29 In another design, the problem was the use of patch porous coating, which
allowed particulate debris to get under the tibial tray, causing subsequent osteolysis and
aseptic failure.30 These design flaws were compounded by the use of thinner
polyethylene liners with inferior wear characteristics and less rigid locking mechanisms,
with higher rates of backside wear compared with contemporary designs.
Early metal-backed noncemented patellar components had higher failure rates than
femoral and tibial components. Most failures were secondary to poor osseointegration
in earlier designs and excessive polyethylene wear because of maltracking.29
Catastrophic failures, including metal-backing dissociation from the polyethylene surface
and peg-baseplate junction dissociation, also were reported.31,32 In addition, a
retrospective review of 211 patients who underwent TKA, with a median follow-up of 37
months, identified five patellar fractures (2.4%), all of which involved a noncemented
component.33 In this study, noncemented implantation and lateral retinacular release
were associated with the fractures; in addition, postoperative osteonecrosis occurred in
two of the five affected knees. Given the frequent failures, noncemented patellar
components fell out of favor, with surgeons often electing to cement a patellar
component in patients with press-fit tibial and femoral components.
Given the high rate of aseptic failure with noncemented designs, particularly on the tibial
and patellar side, many surgeons abandoned their use in favor of more reliable
cemented fixation.
Modern Noncemented Designs
After early failures with noncemented TKA implants, several design changes led to improved
early, midterm, and long-term radiographic and clinical outcomes, renewing interest in the

devices.

Modern Noncemented Designs
Advancements in the technology of porous metals improved early osseointegration in
TKA implants. For example, incorporation of porous tantalum, which contains high
volumetric porosity (ie, 75% to 80%), on the undersurface of the implant increased the
coefficient of friction on cancellous bone compared with previous surfaces while
maintaining a similar modulus of elasticity to cancellous bone to allow for more
physiologic transfer of loading.34,35 In addition, the use of hydroxyapatite surface
coating in some designs has increased not only the shear strength of the fixation
interface but also bone ingrowth in tibial component fixation without the use of
screws.36
In addition to advancements in porous surface technology of TKA implants,
improvements in the geometric design, particularly on the tibial component, have
improved initial stability and fixation. In other models, the use of a keel and cruciform
hexagonal pegs or two hexagonal pegs and a porous tantalum coating has achieved
excellent initial mechanical stability, with limited micromotion and early
osseointegration.37,38 Combined with improved polyethylene liner locking mechanisms,
these implants hold great potential for successful long-term fixation with lower rates of
aseptic loosening and osteolysis.
Surgical Considerations
The ideal indications for noncemented TKA include younger, more active patients and those
with a higher body mass index (Resource 8).
Contraindications include metabolic bone disease, irradiation, and inflammatory arthritis.
To avoid early aseptic failure after noncemented TKA, particular attention must be paid to
accurate bony resections.


Surgical Considerations
Given the excellent long-term outcomes observed with the use of cemented TKA,
identifying the appropriate indications and patient populations for the newer
noncemented components is critical. Younger, more active patients are most likely to
reap the theoretic advantages of long-term osseointegration. In a study of 29 patients
with a mean age of 45 years (range, 34 to 49 years), noncemented TKA components
demonstrated excellent survivorship at midterm follow-up (mean follow-up, 4 years).39
Similar survivorship was demonstrated in a different cohort of 79 patients, all younger
than 60 years, at a mean follow-up of 10 years (range, 8 to 12 years).40 Improved
survivorship of noncemented TKA implants also has been demonstrated in patients with
a body mass index higher than 40 kg/m2, a population that may have experienced
aseptic loosening of a cemented component with higher stresses on the bone-cement
interface.41,42
Contraindications for modern noncemented fixation include patients with a history of
metabolic bone disease or irradiation, which compromises the osteoinductive potential
of the host bone necessary for osseointegration. Similarly, because of the need for
adequate bone stock to support initial press-fit stability, noncemented TKA may be
contraindicated in patients with rheumatoid and other inflammatory forms of arthritis or
cystic bone defects because of unequal bone structure.
The surgical technique used for noncemented TKA is more precise than the technique
used for cemented TKA, requiring highly accurate bone resections to improve implant fit
and bony apposition and minimize shear stress and micromotion. On the femoral side, a
level distal femoral cut is paramount because it drastically affects the plane of the
condylar and chamfer resections. The tibial resection is even less forgiving and requires
an accurately flat resection to achieve perfect bony apposition of the base tray.
Achieving coronal alignment and equal gap balance is key to preventing asymmetric
loading and the potential for tray lift-off. Additional care should be taken to avoid over-
resection of the proximal tibia, which exposes softer metaphyseal bone that is
suboptimal for initial construct stability. Computer navigation or robotic-assisted surgery
ultimately may improve the accuracy of these resections.

On the patellar side, the patella may be left unresurfaced, cemented if substantial wear
or limited bone stock with concerns for maltracking is present, or press-fit with a metal-
backed component in younger patients with adequate bone stock and tracking.
Outcomes of Modern Noncemented TKA
With modern noncemented TKA components, clinical outcomes appear promising and are at
least equivalent to those observed with cemented fixation (Video 3).
Video 3 Meneghini RM: Cementless TKA: The future is now, from Lieberman JR, mod: Hot topics
and controversies in total knee arthroplasty. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, Las Vegas, NV, March 12-16, 2019.

Outcomes of Modern Noncemented TKA
Several early, midterm, and long-term studies have demonstrated similar excellent
radiographic and clinical outcomes with modern noncemented and cemented TKA.

A prospective, randomized clinical trial comparing 65 cemented TKA implants with 76
noncemented TKA implants of the same design demonstrated shorter surgical times in
the noncemented cohort (mean difference, 10 minutes) but similar blood loss, similar
clinical outcome scores, and no substantial radiolucencies between the two groups at 2-
year follow-up. Only one revision procedure was performed for prosthetic joint infection
in the cemented group. All patellae were unresurfaced in this study.38 In a prospective
cohort study on TKA outcomes (minimum follow-up, 5 years) in 100 noncemented knees
versus 312 cemented knees, shorter surgical time was associated with noncemented
TKA (mean difference, 12 minutes); however, similar blood loss and improvements in
Knee Society scores were noted at mid-term follow-up, and no lucencies were present
around any implant. Patellar components were cemented in all patients. Three revision
procedures were performed in the noncemented group; however, none were performed
for aseptic loosening. In the cemented group, two of five revision procedures were
performed for aseptic tibial loosening.43 In another prospective randomized trial
comparing 44 cemented TKA implants with 41 noncemented TKA implants, all with
cemented patellar components, radiographic results and outcome scores were similar
between the two groups at a minimum follow-up of 5 years.44 One revision was noted in
each group, both of which were unrelated to implant fixation.
The long-term results of modern noncemented implants also appear to be encouraging.
In a randomized trial comparing 277 cemented TKA implants with 224 noncemented TKA
implants, with no patellar resurfacing in either group, the aseptic loosening?free
survivorship rate was 95% in both groups at a mean follow-up of 9 years (range, 5.8 to
16.8 years).45 In a randomized trial of 261 patients who underwent bilateral
simultaneous TKA, one cemented and one noncemented, using the same design with all
cemented patellar components, no difference in clinical outcome scores or radiographic
parameters of lucency and alignment were observed at a mean follow-up of 24 years.
The rate of survivorship free of aseptic loosening at 25 years was 98% in both groups.46
Conclusion

Conclusion

After early failures with noncemented TKA implant designs, enhancements in highly
porous surface fabrication and surgical techniques have improved outcomes to match
those of cemented fixation, which is the preferred technique for TKA. Additional studies
on the long-term outcomes of noncemented fixation may lead to the increased use of
these implants for select indications, reaping the theoretic advantages of lifelong biologic
fixation.
